The house on Kettle Lane had three bedrooms, and for ten years Wren had kept two of them shut. Her father's, because he liked it that way. Her brother's, because she did.

She sat at the kitchen table with the promissory note, a legal pad, and a calculator whose seven key stuck. She had done the arithmetic four ways. If she ran every scheduled crossing through June, added the Saturday sunset cruises her father had always refused to do, and sold the old skiff and the spare outboard, she could raise perhaps eleven thousand dollars by the thirtieth. If she sold the house, another sixty, maybe. That left forty-nine thousand dollars and the pier.

Or she could sign Corwin Pell's paper and owe nothing at all.

She wrote that down too, at the bottom of the pad: *Sign. $0.* It looked very clean. It looked like the kind of answer a sensible woman would choose.

She thought about the pier. She thought about her grandfather, whom she had never met, standing chest-deep in the November water to set the pilings. She thought about Mrs. Pruitt's Tuesday dialysis, and the island school's Friday supply run, and the way the whole of Saltmarsh Reach set its clocks by the *Margaret Ann*'s horn. If Pell built his marina, the ferry would move to the town dock, which had no fuel, no parking, and four feet of water at low tide.

Then she thought about forty-nine thousand dollars, and she put her head down on the cool table.

When she lifted it, she went to the hall and picked up the telephone.

She had Tobias's number written inside the back of the phone book, in pencil, the way you'd write down a number for a plumber you never intended to call. It had a Baltimore area code. Her brother had left Saltmarsh Reach ten years ago after a fight with their father so loud the neighbors called Ada, and he had not come back for the funeral. He had sent flowers. White lilies, which their father had hated.

The phone rang six times. A machine picked up. His voice, older, flatter: *You've reached Toby. Leave it at the tone.*

She opened her mouth and nothing came out. The tape hissed. She hung up.

She was still standing in the hall with her hand on the receiver when Ada knocked on the kitchen door. The harbor master had a habit of arriving at the exact moment a person least wanted company, which Wren had come to understand was not an accident.

"You've been doing sums," Ada said, eyeing the legal pad.

"I've been losing at sums."

Ada sat down without being asked and read the pad upside down. She read *Sign. $0.* and her mouth went thin. "Pell came to see you."

"Yesterday. On the boat."

"He's been to see half the waterfront. The Gundersons. The Lees at the boatyard. The fish co-op." Ada tapped the table. "He needs the council to rezone the whole harbor front for his marina. The vote's set for the first of June, a Monday. If it passes, every lot on the water triples, and anybody who's behind on anything sells to him at his price. If it fails, his project's dead in the water, and so is his reason for wanting your pier."

Wren looked at her. "So if the vote fails—"

"Then you still owe him a hundred and twenty thousand dollars," Ada said. "But he doesn't want the pier anymore. He wants his money. And men who want money can be negotiated with. Men who want land can't."

"Can the vote fail?"

"Five councilors. Two for, two against, and Marguerite Okafor sitting on the fence like a gull, waiting to see which way the fish are running." Ada stood and buttoned her coat. "Your father used to be able to move Marguerite. Folks listened to him."

"I'm not him."

"No," Ada agreed. "You're the one who's still here."

After she left, Wren went back to the hall and dialed the Baltimore number again. This time, when the tone sounded, she said, "Toby. It's Wren. Dad left a mess. I could use you." She paused. "You don't have to call back."

He didn't.
